title: A House of Dynamite
synopsis: An ICBM has been launched from somewhere — they don't know where yet — at the United States. You are the Deputy National Security Adviser. You have eighteen minutes before you have to advise.

nodes.text: The Watch Officer's voice goes flat: 'Single SBIRS detection, ballistic, transpacific.' Your coffee, half-raised, goes back to the desk. You have eighteen minutes.

choices.text: Call STRATCOM first
choices.consequence: Verify before you wake the President.

choices.text: Wake the President first
choices.consequence: Time is the thing you can't make.

nodes.text: STRATCOM confirms: it's real, on a depressed trajectory, single warhead estimate. Origin: somewhere in the Sea of Okhotsk box. Not enough to assign blame yet.

choices.text: Demand a confidence interval
Order a second sensor handoff

nodes.text: The President is on the line in 90 seconds. He sounds awake in the way only certain men sound awake at 4 a.m. 'Talk to me,' he says.

choices.text: Brief plainly with what you know
Brief carefully with caveats

nodes.text: Confidence is up to 87% real. Origin narrowed but not assigned. Three candidate countries. Two of them are nuclear states. One of them is not.

choices.text: Insist on confirmed attribution before recommendation
Begin contingency planning for all three
choices.consequence: Be ready for whatever the attribution says.

nodes.text: Your Chinese counterpart — your hard-earned channel — answers your secure line. He is, audibly, also at 4 a.m. He says, 'Not us. Verify.'

choices.text: Trust the channel and move on
Press him for one piece of corroborating data

nodes.text: GBI — ground-based interceptors — are ready. The Pacific intercept window is narrowing. You can fire to attempt intercept now or hold for better track confidence.

choices.text: Authorize the interceptor shot now
choices.consequence: Try to break it before the math is done.

choices.text: Hold for better track
choices.consequence: Don't waste the few shots you have.

nodes.text: An Air Force colonel reminds the room that the President has authorized 'consultative' — not full launch — until he formally elects. The distinction is paper-thin in eighteen minutes.

choices.text: Get the President on with the war cabinet now
Hold the war cabinet — let him think one more minute
choices.consequence: Sometimes a quiet minute saves a city.

nodes.text: GBI fires. The room watches a screen that updates every two seconds. The hit is a possible. The hit is, after a long pause, a miss. The room becomes very quiet.

choices.text: Authorize second shot
choices.consequence: Three shots in the magazine; spend.

choices.text: Hold for the final shot
choices.consequence: Save the last one for terminal phase.

nodes.text: Attribution lands. NSA and a second source converge: a rogue North Korean unit. Not state-sanctioned. The North Korean leadership themselves are, allegedly, asking on a back channel what's happening.

choices.text: Open the back channel directly
Treat the launch as state action until proven otherwise

nodes.text: Second GBI: miss. The room is now praying without saying so. The President is on the line and quietly asking for one piece of advice he can take into the next sentence of his life.

choices.text: Tell him: no retaliatory launch, no matter what
Tell him: hold response posture, but reassure allies

nodes.text: Back channel runs cold for ninety seconds and then a North Korean general — terrified — confirms the rogue unit, says they've moved to shut them down, asks for the U.S. not to escalate. He sounds like he means it.

choices.text: Trust him on the call alone
Demand a verifiable action in 60 seconds

nodes.text: Third GBI: hit. The warhead is destroyed over the Pacific. The room exhales. Then it goes cold again — there is debris, and there is the question of what happens next.

choices.text: Order a public, calm statement immediately
Hold all statements for the next hour

nodes.text: Third GBI: miss. The warhead is in terminal phase. The trajectory is — by some appalling stroke — into open ocean three hundred miles west of the coast. Detonation is in twenty seconds.

choices.text: Brace the rooms for the message
choices.consequence: Be the calm in the room.

choices.text: Order DEFCON 2 immediately

nodes.text: Either the world stays the same or it doesn't. Either way, the next sentence the President says will matter forever. He looks at you. He has, all night, been looking at you when he didn't know who else to look at.

choices.text: Recommend public reassurance and quiet diplomacy
Recommend a measured demonstration of resolve

nodes.text: Whatever happens, you have done what is, perhaps, the most consequential job in the country tonight. Your hands have started shaking only now. You hide them under the table.

choices.text: Stay in the room for the next twelve hours
Hand off to the senior team and rest

nodes.text: The President addresses the nation. The wording — yours — is, against all instinct, calm and exact. The country, somehow, listens. The night becomes a memory the country tells slightly wrong for the rest of its life.

choices.text: Stay in office for the rebuild
Resign in a year, on your own terms
choices.consequence: Spend the political capital and leave.

nodes.text: The country survives. The agencies don't all behave well in the after. You testify, you correct, you fight institutional fights you didn't think you'd have to. It is, in its own way, a second long night.

choices.text: Push for non-proliferation reforms
Speak at the memorial when the year turns
choices.consequence: First the dead, then the doctrine.

nodes.text: Sun on the lawn, coffee that's cold. The President asks you to draft a paragraph he can build a year on. You realize the next move decides which legacy you carry — the one that stayed or the one that left.

choices.text: Draft the paragraph for a long policy season
Draft the paragraph for a clean handoff

nodes.text: Under the cameras you make the case that the system that worked tonight should be the system that's never tested again. The committee leans in. You decide which reform to spend your credibility on.

choices.text: Spend it on weapons
Spend it on the warning architecture

nodes.text: A year on, a small memorial at the Navy Yard for the analysts who held the line that night. You speak for two minutes. You realize, after, that one of those minutes is what the next decade of your work should sound like.

choices.text: Turn the speech into a policy push
Turn the speech into your private vow

nodes.text: Two years later you stand in a room signing a treaty that, in part, exists because of that night. It is incomplete and necessary. You are old now. You sleep, mostly. The nightmares come less.
You leave on your own terms and teach at a school you can pronounce. Your students do not know what you did that night. You tell them the lessons without the story. The lessons survive. So do you.

The reforms slow the next escalation. Slow is not the same as stopped. You are, after a decade, both more cynical and more hopeful — a strange pair that, you realize, has always been the truth about your job.
You spend the rest of your career making sure the system that woke you that night will, one day, wake fewer people. You will not be the one to use it. That is, you decide, the right kind of legacy.
